pitch.title: An allowance for your agent.
pitch.subtitle: Autonomous payments. Spending you can account for.
pitch.narration: An agent can send a payment in milliseconds. But who decides how much it spends, which sellers it trusts, and when a retry loop should stop? Wallie puts an allowance in front of the payment. It's an open-source runtime for agents that buy data, compute, and services over x402. This submission brings that runtime to Solana.

pitch.title: A wallet balance is not a spending policy.
pitch.subtitle: Check the destination, the price, the rate, and the remaining allowance before signing.
pitch.narration: A funded wallet tells an agent what it can afford. It doesn't tell it what it's allowed to spend. Wallie checks the destination, the price of each call, the rate of spending, and the allowance that's left, all before it signs. An operator can pause everything with a kill switch. These limits cover the payments Wallie routes, not some unrelated cloud bill.

pitch.title: A fixed price. Or a metered ceiling.
pitch.subtitle: exact pays the quoted amount. upto settles actual usage and returns the difference.
pitch.narration: There are two ways to pay. Exact is a fixed price for a single API call. Up-to opens a Solana payment channel with a ceiling you approve, then settles only what the request actually uses. Our public devnet run deposited ten cents, charged three, and returned seven. The transaction is finalized and linked from this page, so judges can check it straight on Solana.

pitch.title: Locked money is still committed money.
pitch.subtitle: Available allowance = funded budget − spent − reserved − escrowed.
pitch.narration: Money sitting in a channel isn't free to spend again. Wallie counts it as escrow. The budget, the ledger, the dashboard, and the agent tools all read the same channel records. If a receipt goes missing, recovery keeps the payment in the history. If the outcome is unclear, the deposit stays held. A corrupt state file stops new spending instead of quietly resetting the allowance.

pitch.title: One runtime. A visible payment history.
pitch.subtitle: SDK · CLI · MCP · local dashboard
pitch.narration: Developers reach it through the SDK, the command line, or the MCP server. The included example drives the real MCP protocol: it buys an exact API on the local practice rail, makes a metered Solana request offline, and hits a spending limit on purpose. The offline demo needs no keys. A separate devnet canary proves the on-chain metered path. Sellers get payment middleware and a worker that cleans up abandoned channels.

pitch.title: A small payment. A complete audit trail.
pitch.subtitle: Open source under MIT · github.com/fskroes/AllowanceKit
pitch.narration: This submission ships the source, a repeatable local demo, regression tests, a full walkthrough, and a public devnet transaction. The evidence keeps local simulation separate from real settlement, and it doesn't claim Solana mainnet as tested production traffic. Start with the demo, read the ledger, and follow the explorer link. Wallie gives an agent room to act while keeping every payment inside the allowance its operator set.

walkthrough.title: Start with no keys and no real money.
walkthrough.subtitle: Node 24 or later · npm ci · npm run demo:mcp
walkthrough.narration: This walkthrough keeps the repeatable offline demo separate from the public devnet payment. Start from the source with Node 24 or later. Run npm ci, then npm run demo:mcp. No wallet key, no funded account. The script starts local sellers and connects a client to the real MCP server. Every terminal excerpt you see is captured from that command, not typed up for the video.

walkthrough.title: The client discovers the payment tools.
walkthrough.subtitle: The same policy and ledger are used by the SDK, CLI, and MCP server.
walkthrough.narration: First the client asks the server for its tools and its budget. pay_fetch is the tool for calling a paid API. get_budget shows what's funded, spent, reserved, and locked in channels. list_channels shows every deposit and its state. The server also exposes approval and reclaim actions. Any client that holds approval authority has to be trusted with it, and the spending rules still apply to every attempt.

walkthrough.title: An exact call buys weather data.
walkthrough.subtitle: Local practice rail · exact scheme · $0.001
walkthrough.narration: The first purchase is weather data for a tenth of a cent. This runs on the local practice rail, so its transaction id is not evidence of a Solana payment. The request gets a payment challenge, the runtime authorizes the amount, and the local seller settles it. The client receives the API response together with the cost. It's the exact flow and its policy boundary, with no external services.

walkthrough.title: The expensive request stops before payment.
walkthrough.subtitle: $5 request · $1 per-call cap · blocked
walkthrough.narration: Next the agent tries the five-dollar enterprise feed. The per-call cap is one dollar, so Wallie returns a structured block with a plain explanation, and nothing is paid. The client can take the quoted price and the cap and pick something cheaper, or stop. A refusal is part of the normal result, so the agent doesn't have to catch an exception to understand what happened.

walkthrough.title: Authorize the ceiling before opening.
walkthrough.subtitle: Solana devnet transaction format · offline seller simulation
walkthrough.narration: The second phase switches to the Solana runtime and a metered seller. The ceiling is ten cents, and each row costs a tenth of a cent. The buyer builds the Solana channel transaction from a pinned block hash, while the seller simulates settlement locally. This part is deliberately offline. The same buyer and seller run against public devnet in the recorded canary later in this video.

walkthrough.title: $0.10 deposited. $0.03 used. $0.07 returned.
walkthrough.subtitle: Thirty rows at $0.001 each
walkthrough.narration: The request reads thirty rows. The real charge is three cents, and the unused seven cents goes back to the allowance. The response shows both amounts and the channel id. The ledger stores what was paid, the original deposit, and the refund together. Every value is an integer in micro-units, never floating point. The channel closes, and the budget reflects three cents, not the ten-cent ceiling.

walkthrough.title: A missing receipt must not reset the budget.
walkthrough.subtitle: Durable channel state · idempotent settlement accounting · conservative uncertainty
walkthrough.narration: Now picture a request that settles on-chain but loses its HTTP receipt. Recovery records that charge before it frees the rest of the allowance, and it won't record the same payment twice when a late receipt arrives. The tests cover those edges. If the chain can't confirm the result, the deposit stays committed. A corrupt channel file raises an error and blocks new spending instead of resetting the account.

walkthrough.title: Cleanup survives a process restart.
walkthrough.subtitle: Persistent library state · automatic worker · explicit sweep and shutdown
walkthrough.narration: Seller recovery uses the payment-channel library's own cleanup manager. Wallie persists its channel state, starts the worker, and gives you a shutdown path and an explicit sweep command. A failed settlement doesn't become a successful charge just because a retry ran. Abandoned deposits follow the program's timeout and refund rules. Tests cover the worker's lifecycle and persistence across a restart. Seller keys stay in the environment, out of the saved state.

walkthrough.title: The public devnet settlement is finalized.
walkthrough.subtitle: Slot 498210157 · no transaction error · seller +$0.03 · buyer +$0.07 refund
walkthrough.narration: This is the separate public Solana devnet proof. The recorded transaction finalized at slot 498210157, with no error. Its token-balance changes show thirty thousand micro-units going to the seller and seventy thousand coming back to the buyer. The submission links the full transaction and the exact canary command. These numbers were read from Solana's own RPC, not lifted from a screenshot.

walkthrough.title: Source, demo, tests, and transaction proof.
walkthrough.subtitle: Run npm test · inspect docs/submission · follow the explorer link
walkthrough.narration: The hand-in package pulls it together: an install path, the source, the local MCP demo, the canary record, this walkthrough, and the short pitch. Run the tests and the build, then trace the money through the ledger and channel modules. The demo page marks which results are local and which are on-chain. That's the whole story: an agent that buys a service, respects a limit, and accounts for the money afterward.
